analysis.one_liner: Designates new Montana wilderness areas while releasing roadless forests to logging and mandating a land swap for Plum Creek Timber.
analysis.headline: The bill never left a Senate subcommittee and died when the 101st Congress ended, so its roughly 620,000 acres of new wilderness, its release of roadless forests, and its Plum Creek land exchange all never happened.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill was a package trade over Montana's federal forests. It would put about 620,000 acres of national forest into the National Wilderness Preservation System, where roads, logging, and most development are banned. At the same time it would release at least 328,000 acres of roadless national forest from wilderness consideration, opening them to logging, mining, and road building, and would strip courts of the power to review those decisions. It would also write into law a land swap with Plum Creek Timber Company: the government would hand the company about 21,600 acres of national forest land, $3.4 million in cash, road easements, and mineral rights, in exchange for about 46,000 acres of company land, with formal appraisals of the minerals waived and environmental review declared unnecessary. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, Plum Creek Timber Company would have gained federal land, cash, road easements, and mineral interests under legislatively fixed terms. Logging and mining interests would have gained access to roadless national forest freed from wilderness review. Ranchers with existing grazing allotments would have kept grazing in the new wilderness areas. Outdoor recreationists and conservationists would also have gained permanent protection for roughly 620,000 acres, including the Great Burn and Scotchman Peaks country.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Plum Creek Timber and logging interests

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have designated about 620,000 acres across 17 named areas as wilderness, permanently barring roads, logging, and most development there.
It would have folded the Great Bear and Scapegoat Wilderness Areas into the Bob Marshall Wilderness as one consolidated area.

It would have added about 46,000 acres of Plum Creek land to the national forests, including tracts in and next to the Hyalite-Porcupine-Buffalo Horn Wilderness Study Area and the Scapegoat Wilderness.
It would have guaranteed that existing livestock grazing and allotments continue inside the newly designated wilderness, and allowed water- and weather-data collection devices in wilderness.

It would have ended the decades-old wilderness study status of Montana roadless lands by releasing them for 'multiple use' management, which in practice means timber harvest, mineral development, and road construction under the forest plans.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would have conveyed about 21,600 acres of national forest plus $3.4 million and federal mineral rights to Plum Creek, with the bill declaring the mineral exchange exempt from the National Environmental Policy Act and stating that no formal appraisal of the minerals was required, leaving valuation risk with the public. People who value quiet, roadless public forest would have lost at least 328,000 acres to development-oriented management, and the bill would have barred courts from reviewing those decisions.

drawbacks.text: The roadless-area release would have opened at least 328,000 acres to logging, mining, and road building, and would have declared the wilderness analyses in the forest plans off-limits to judicial review, cutting off the main legal avenue citizens have to challenge forest decisions.

The Plum Creek exchange was hard-wired in statute: about 21,600 acres of federal land plus $3.4 million in cash for the company, with mineral interests swapped without a formal appraisal and the whole deal declared not a major federal environmental action, so any mispricing would fall on taxpayers rather than on a reviewing agency or court.

The wilderness designations would permanently end motorized access, mechanized recreation, and any resource development in those areas, a real cost to some adjacent communities and users that supporters accept in exchange for permanent protection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a genuine trade: roughly 620,000 acres of permanent wilderness in exchange for releasing hundreds of thousands of roadless acres to development and handing a named company a legislatively mandated, lightly reviewed land deal. The wilderness gains were real and large, but the release clause and the Plum Creek sections stripped the normal checks — judicial review, environmental assessment, and appraisal — that usually protect the public's side of a bargain. As written, the oversight savings were the point, and they cut against ordinary citizens, not for them.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate's energy committee referred it to its public lands subcommittee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Conrad Burns introduced the bill on March 6, 1990, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
The next day it was referred to the subcommittee on Public Lands, National Parks, where it stayed.
A star print (an updated printed version) of the bill was ordered on April 4, 1990; no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the roadless lands kept their existing protections and litigation rights, the Plum Creek exchange stayed voluntary and reviewable rather than legislatively mandated, and no federal land or cash went to the company. The cost is that the roughly 620,000 acres of proposed wilderness also never gained permanent protection.

for.name: Conrad Burns
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, its sole sponsor, and got it printed in updated form; it received no further action.

for.name: Plum Creek Timber Company, L.P.
for.role: Private timberland owner named in the bill as the exchange counterparty
for.what_they_did: Had agreed in principle with the Department of Agriculture to the severed-minerals exchange that Title III would make law.

against.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its public lands subcommittee and never held a hearing or markup on it.

against.name: Senate Subcommittee on Public Lands, National Parks
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 7, 1990 and took no action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had a single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors in a Democratic-led Senate, so the record shows no partisan pattern either way.

industries.note: The bill would have mandated, by name, a swap giving the company about 21,600 acres of national forest land, $3.4 million in cash, road easements, and federal mineral interests, with mineral appraisals waived and environmental review declared inapplicable. The public would have received company land including wild-study-area inholdings, but the company's side of the deal was fixed in statute rather than left to normal agency valuation and review.

Releasing roadless national forest to multiple-use management opens it to timber sales and road construction, and the bill barred courts from reviewing the wilderness analyses behind those decisions. Quiet-use recreation on those lands loses when logging access arrives.

Released roadless acres become available for mineral development under the forest plans, and federal oil and gas lease rights would have vested directly in Plum Creek when existing leases ended. The mineral exchange section also loosened normal appraisal and environmental requirements.

The bill requires that existing livestock grazing and allotments continue and be administered inside the newly designated wilderness, locking in grazing's place in areas that otherwise carry the strictest protection federal land law offers.

Designating roughly 620,000 acres as wilderness would have permanently protected it from roads, logging, and development, the outcome that community has sought in Montana for decades. Their gain came bundled with losses elsewhere in the same bill.
